Today

Every session gets a status, a note, and a signature before you log off. Three minutes at the start, five at the end, and the session log in between if you find it useful — it's a scratchpad, not a requirement. When you get stuck on how to do something, the Cheat sheet tab has the click-by-click for all of it.

Keeping your own record. This page clears itself on a schedule — Today resets overnight, This week on Monday morning, Month end on the 1st. So if you want to keep a record, take a copy before it clears: Save a copy of this page at the bottom opens your print dialog, where you choose Save as PDF and name it with the date. Everything you've ticked and typed is captured, with your name and the date across the top. Then the page rolls over on its own and you're back to blank — nothing to undo. Start fresh is there if you want to clear it early.

          Cheat sheet

          In the order they tend to come up. Steps marked with Jane's own wording are taken from Jane's published guides and link back to them. The sand-coloured boxes are ours to fill in — they hold the parts only Beachside can answer.

          Read 14 first if you have ever written a note inside a treatment plan, or from the Chart tab. A SOAP note and a treatment plan are not the same place in Jane. A note written in the wrong one is complete, signed, and invisible to the schedule and to every report — which means it looks to everyone else like you never wrote it. This is how Jane is built rather than something broken, and it takes about thirty seconds to put right once you know where to click. See item 14 below.
          01Getting Kaiser to send the TPIs — the Lucet calendar, set once›
          How it actually works. The TPI is not a Jane form. Kaiser sends it to the client automatically, 30 minutes before each scheduled appointment — but only for appointments that exist on Lucet (polestarapp.com, headed "Lucet Admin"; some of us call it Tridium). No Lucet appointment, no TPI. Nobody sends anything by hand.

          So the whole job is putting your Kaiser clients on the Lucet calendar as a repeating appointment, once, and giving the series a sensible end date.

          Checked in Lucet on 31 August — and three of these fields were not where we thought. The address is polestarapp.com with no www (the www version returns "No configuration found"). SCHEDULING opens the calendar, and clicking an empty slot gives a CREATE APPOINTMENT box containing, in this order: Event Type, Site, Provider, Site Timezone, Start Time, End Time, Patient Name, Patient Timezone, Repeat, Visit Type, In person / Virtual appointment, Notes, then CANCEL and CREATE.

          Assessment Type, the Notifications section with its Assessments and Appointments columns, and the consent tick box did not appear on that form. They may only surface once a patient is selected, or they may live on the patient's own record. Since the Assessments box is what actually controls the TPI, this matters — work through steps 5 to 7 below carefully next time you set one up, and tell Kerry where those fields really are so this can be corrected.
          Setting one up — the fields that matter
          1. Repeat — tick it, then choose the pattern, e.g. Weekly on Thursday.
          2. Ends — set On Date and put the date at least a year out. When a series ends, the TPIs stop with no warning of any kind.
          3. Visit Type — e.g. Psychotherapy - 60 min.
          4. In person or Virtual appointment — pick the one that's true. It should match how you've set the session up in Jane.
          5. Assessment Type → TPI. This is the field that decides whether a TPI is sent at all. Get everything else right and leave this wrong, and nothing goes out.
          6. Notifications — check the client's email and mobile are current, then tick the boxes. There are two columns, Assessments and Appointments, for each of email and text. Assessments is the TPI. Appointments ticked and Assessments blank is the single easiest way to get this wrong, and it looks completely normal.
          7. Tick Patient has provided consent to make this change — Lucet won't save without it, and all notifications go to whatever contact details you've just entered.
          8. Add anything worth knowing in Notes, then save.
          Checking whether it actually landed — you can see this
          1. Click PATIENTS and click the client's name to open their record.
          2. Find the ASSESSMENTS tab.
          3. Every assessment ever sent is listed, newest first, with the appointment it belonged to.
          Two shortcuts found on 31 August. The PATIENTS list has a Last Assessment column — often that answers the question without opening anything — and a Launch column whose paper icon sends or launches an assessment for that person directly. The patient record itself opens on ALERTS, a BHI SCORE dial with a trend arrow, and score tiles for AOQ, PHQ, GAD and AUD, each dated and colour-dotted. Kaiser's Clinical Documentation Requirements — the 72-hour Initial Evaluation and the rest of cheat sheet 12 — are printed further down that same record, so you never have to remember them.

          Read the second column — it tells you the outcome in one word:

          • Completed — they filled it in. A VIEW link opens it, and the scores appear on the right: BHI, PHQ, GAD, AUD, TA, AOQ, DRG and C-SSRS, colour-dotted by severity.
          • Expired — it was sent and never filled in. The row shows the date and time it expired.
          The window is short, and this is the part to understand. Lucet schedules the send shortly before the appointment and the assessment expires at around the appointment start time. So a client who opens it after you've begun has almost certainly missed it. That's the mechanism behind the "they never filled it in" problem — not forgetfulness, a twenty-minute window. If getting these completed matters, the conversation to have with clients is "watch for it just before we start," not "please do it beforehand."
          An empty week is not automatically a fault. Kaiser generates one TPI per patient per week across all their providers — if the client completed one at another appointment earlier in the week, none is generated for yours. Check that before assuming something is broken.
          When a TPI genuinely is missing, check in this order: the Assessments tab, to see whether one was sent and whether it expired; then Assessment Type is set to TPI; then the Assessments notification box is ticked on email or text; then the email and phone on file are the ones they actually use. It is nearly always one of those, not the client.
          On an existing appointment you can
          • EDIT — change the time, the service, or the recurrence
          • CANCEL APPOINTMENT
          • MARK AS NO SHOW
          The rule that keeps this working: if you change it in Jane, change it in Lucet. These are two separate calendars and nothing syncs them. Move a client to a new day in Jane and forget Lucet, and Kaiser keeps sending TPIs 30 minutes before an appointment that no longer exists — while the real session gets none. Terminate a client in Jane only, and the series keeps firing until its end date. Every time you use cheat sheet 8, 9 or 10 on a Kaiser client, do it twice.
          Watch the recurrence end date. A series that ends stops producing TPIs silently — no warning, no error, the client simply stops getting them. When you set one up, put the end date at least a year out, and note that series set up together all expire together.
          02The client didn't fill out the TPI before session — activating it live›
          The TPI is not in Jane — don't go looking for it there. Kaiser sent it to the client's own phone or inbox 30 minutes before this session, triggered by the Lucet appointment (cheat sheet 01). So it already exists and it is already with them.
          Before you chase it — check whether one is even due. Kaiser generates one TPI per patient per week, across every provider they see. If your client saw their doctor on Monday and completed a TPI then, no second one is generated for your Thursday session. That is working correctly, not a failure. Nothing to fix, nothing to chase.
          If one is due and they haven't done it — launch it in the session
          1. Open the client's record in Lucet.
          2. Click + ADD ASSESSMENT.
          3. Choose the option to launch it in the session.
          4. Work through the questions with the client, there and then.

          On telehealth, share your screen so the client can read the questions and answer as you go, rather than listening to you read a scale aloud. It keeps the wording standard, which matters for a measure, and it turns an interruption into something you do together.

          This is the reliable route, and it's better than asking them to hunt for an email — the sent version expires around the appointment start time anyway, so by the time you've noticed, theirs has usually lapsed.

          If it should have been sent and wasn't
          1. Check the Assessments tab — was one sent at all, and did it expire?
          2. Check the appointment entry: does today's appointment exist, is Assessment Type set to TPI, is the Assessments notification box ticked, and are the email and mobile on file current?
          3. Fix whatever's wrong today — a broken entry affects every future session in that run, not just this one.
          Everything below is for Jane's own measures — PHQ-9, GAD-7, ACE — not the TPI
          Jane keeps its measures in two places. An Intake Form is the once-at-the-start paperwork. A Clinical Survey is a measure collected repeatedly through care — that's where PHQ-9, ACE and GAD-7 live.
          Sending a Clinical Survey
          1. Open the client's profile and find Surveys in the lower right.
          2. Click Set Up and pick the survey from the dropdown.
          3. To do it right now: Email sends it to them immediately; Fill out lets you complete it on their behalf, or hand them your device to do it themselves.
          4. To stop chasing it every time, set the sending method to Before or after an appointment — you choose how far ahead it goes out and how many times — or On regular intervals for a daily, weekly or monthly cadence.
          The one to warn people about: if you hand your device to the client to fill it in, Jane logs you out when they finish. You'll need to log back in. Fine if you know it's coming, alarming mid-session if you don't.

          Completed surveys land in the client's Charts tab, dated by submission, and clients can see them in their portal under Documents.

          If it's set up as an Intake Form instead
          1. Client's profile → Profile tab → Online Intake Forms.
          2. Fill Out to do it together, or Email to send it now.

          Sources: Jane — Clinical Surveys · Creating & Sending a Manual Intake Form

          All Clinical Surveys are now switched on for every staff member (27 Aug), so PHQ-9, GAD-7, ACE and the Child and Teen Self Assessments are in everyone's list. If a survey isn't showing for you, say so rather than working around it.
          03Uploading a handwritten note instead of typing it twice›

          The short version: photograph or scan the page, drop it into a chart entry, answer the template questions in the same entry, sign once.

          From your computer
          1. Open the client's Chart tab.
          2. Click New Chart Entry.
          3. Choose File/Image from the list.
          4. Click Add Image/File and pick your scan.
          5. Give it a clear title with the date.
          6. Click Sign.
          From your phone, during or right after session
          1. Open Jane in your phone's browser and tap the appointment in Day view.
          2. Tap New Chart Entry and choose the Image/File Upload option.
          3. Take the picture — it uploads straight into the chart.
          4. Then delete the photo from your camera roll. Jane warns the image stays on the phone otherwise.
          To get the upload and the questions in one signable entry: the template needs a File/Image Upload part built into it (it's under "Charting on Images" when you add items to a template). Then the entry holds the scan and the template questions together, and one signature covers both. Templates without that part can't have an upload dropped in on the fly.
          Open question for the practice: none of our templates is known to carry a File/Image Upload part yet. Until one does, an uploaded scan is a separate chart entry from the entry holding the template questions — two entries, two signatures, for one session. Adding the part to Beachside SOAP Note would collapse that back into one, and is probably worth doing before this goes out to everyone.

          Limits: 50 MB per file. PDF is best for scans — screen resolution is plenty, don't scan at high DPI. Filenames can't be changed after upload.

          Sources: Scanning & Uploading to Jane Charts · Charting on a Mobile Device · Chart Parts

          04Which template to use, and what each one is for›

          Templates live per staff member: Staff → your name → Templates. Jane shares new templates with the whole clinic automatically, and each of you uses the toggle beside a template to show or hide it in your own list. They always sort alphabetically — you can't drag them into your own order, so the name is what makes one findable.

          Check your toggles before you go looking for a template. A template that's toggled off simply isn't in your list when you chart — it hasn't been deleted, you just can't see it. Several of ours ship toggled off, including the AI one. Toggles are per staff profile, so the on/off column below is one person's view, not the practice's — check your own the first time you use this page.
          Template name in JaneUse it forOn by default?
          There is no Kaiser-specific template. Every one of these is general. If Kaiser needs anything the standard note doesn't capture, that's a template to build and label plainly — "Kaiser — progress note", so it sorts beside its siblings. Templates sort alphabetically and can't be reordered, so the name is the whole filing system.

          Source: Jane — Chart Templates: Creating, Editing and Deleting

          05Transcribe → SOAP note → the questions underneath → sign›
          This all happens inside HIPAA-compliant software. The recording, the transcription and the note stay within Jane — nothing is sent to a consumer AI tool, and Jane states the data isn't used to train AI models. Say that plainly if a client asks; it's the honest answer and it's usually the reassurance they're looking for.
          Consent first, every time. Compliant software does not remove the need to ask. Jane's own guidance: ask the client before you record, and they can withdraw consent at any point. Jane doesn't capture that consent for you — put it in the intake form or record it in the note.
          Use the right template or nothing happens. Transcribe only works in a chart entry built on a template that carries a Smart SOAP Note part. Ours is "Beachside SOAP Note- for use with AI" — and it ships toggled off. Turn it on first under Staff → your name → Templates. If transcribe has ever seemed broken for you, this is almost certainly why.
          Before it will work at all

          If you're building your own template, the part is added under Staff → your name → Templates → Add Item → Smart SOAP Note. The prompt field is where you tell it SOAP vs DAP vs BIRP, and narrative vs point form.

          In person
          1. Open the client's Chart tab and the entry with your Smart SOAP Note.
          2. Click the microphone icon at the top of the entry.
          3. Click Record Audio and allow microphone access.
          4. Pick your mic, check the bars are moving, click Start Record.
          5. A banner follows you around Jane — pause or finish from there. Recording stops on its own at 90 minutes, with a warning at 80.
          Telehealth
          1. Join the call as usual.
          2. Click Transcribe at the bottom of the screen. A recording symbol appears in the upper left — the client sees it too.
          3. Stop pauses; Transcribe resumes.
          4. Click End Call. Jane then asks you to pick a template or add the summary to an existing draft.
          After the note is generated — this is the part that gets skipped
          What Jane is doing, and what it is not. Jane transcribes the session much like a court reporter would, then writes that transcript up in SOAP format. It is a machine's account of what was said. Verifying it for accuracy is the therapist's responsibility — read every line and correct anything that is wrong, missing, or misattributed. You are signing it, so it becomes your clinical record and your words, whoever typed them first.
          And you get one chance. Once the note is generated, the transcription is automatically deleted. There is no going back to check what was actually said. If the note is wrong and you sign it, the only record of that session is the wrong one — so verify before you move on, not next week.
          The AI writes the SOAP. The form is yours. Sitting above the generated SOAP is a form of questions, and every one of them has to be answered, for every session. AI Scribe does not touch it and never will. A note with a beautiful SOAP and a blank form is an incomplete note.
          1. Read the generated SOAP line by line and correct it. This is verification, not proofreading — the transcript it came from is already gone.
          2. Fill out the whole form above it. Client Location, and every other question on it.
          3. Click Sign at the bottom right, then OK. The padlock closes.
          Client Location is the telehealth one to watch. Checked 31 August: it sits on the standard Beachside SOAP Note as well as the AI one, so it needs answering on every session note, not only transcribed ones. It records where the client physically was — not where you were. It matters for licensure and for knowing where to send help in an emergency, and it's a required field, so the note won't be complete without it. Jane has no such field out of the box; ours is there because it was built into the template deliberately.

          Sources: AI Scribe: Recording a Session · Transcribe a Telehealth Appointment · Billing Telehealth Claims (US)

          06One reschedule per weekly session — and how to note it when it gets billed›
          Noting it in Jane
          1. Move the appointment (see 08) rather than cancelling and rebooking — the booking history stays intact.
          2. Open the appointment panel and type into Add Note…, then click Add. Say what happened plainly: "Reschedule #2 this week — original time billed per policy."
          3. The note shows as a speech bubble in the corner of the appointment on the Schedule. It's internal — clients never see it.
          Tested 31 August, and this is the finding that matters most on this page: we cannot bill a late cancellation in Jane today. Opening Cancel/Delete on a real appointment gives only three things — a heading Cancel with Notifications, one option under it called Cancel Appointment - No Charge, a link reading Set up Late Cancellations Fees, and under a second heading Without notifications, Delete Appointment.

          There is no fee to choose and no Reason for Cancellation dropdown, because no late cancellation fees have been created in the account. Until somebody sets them up, every cancellation you record is a no-charge one, whatever the policy says. Kerry needs to know this — the missed-session policy is currently unenforceable in Jane.
          When the second one has to be billed — not possible yet
          1. Click the original appointment → Cancel/Delete.
          2. Today the only option is Cancel Appointment - No Charge. Take it, and write what happened in a note so the money question can be picked up later.
          3. Once fees exist, a Late Cancellation option will appear in this same menu — the link Set up Late Cancellations Fees in that menu is where they get created.
          A late cancellation and an ordinary cancellation are different things in Jane: the late one carries an invoice, the ordinary one doesn't, and only staff can do a late cancellation. The fees themselves are set up once under Settings → Fees.

          Sources: Late Cancellations · No Show & Late Cancellation Fees · Special Notes

          07Tracking the two free cancellations — the workaround›

          Straight answer: Jane has no per-appointment label or custom tag you can set to "first cancellation / second cancellation." Jane's "Tags" are only for controlling online booking, and appointment colours come from the treatment, not the appointment. So it's a workaround — but a good one, in two halves.

          The convention — one starred note per client, kept current

          Everyone writes it the same way, so anyone opening the chart can read the count in a second:

          Free cancellations: 1 of 2 used (14 Aug)

          First free cancellation — step by step
          1. On the Schedule, click the appointment being cancelled.
          2. Click Cancel/Delete.
          3. Pick a Reason for Cancellation from the dropdown, or Other Reason to type one.
          4. Do not apply a fee — this one is free.
          5. Click Save & Cancel Appointment.
          6. Now open any future appointment for that client.
          7. Type into Add Note…: Free cancellations: 1 of 2 used (14 Aug). Click Add.
          8. Click the star to the right of the note. Star and note turn orange, and it now appears on all of that client's future appointments — so the next person to open the chart sees the count without going looking.
          Second free cancellation — step by step
          1. Cancel exactly as above, with a reason and no fee.
          2. Open a future appointment and find the starred note.
          3. Notes can't be edited — the three-dot menu beside a note offers Delete only. So: add the replacement first, then delete the old one.
          4. Type the new note: Free cancellations: 2 of 2 used (14 Aug, 3 Sep) — next cancellation is billable. Click Add.
          5. Star the new note.
          6. Then click the three dots beside the old note and choose Delete. Do it in that order, so the client is never sitting with no count on file.
          Third cancellation onward — supposed to be billable
          It cannot be billed in Jane right now. Checked 31 August: the Cancel/Delete menu offers only Cancel Appointment - No Charge, plus a link to Set up Late Cancellations Fees — because no fees exist in the account yet. Cancel with no charge, then write the note below so the amount can be recovered later once fees are in place.
          1. Click the appointment → Cancel/Delete → Cancel Appointment - No Charge.
          2. Add a note recording what should have happened: Cancellation 3 — billable per policy, not charged (fees not set up in Jane) (18 Sep). No need to star this one; the starred count note already tells the story.
          Only staff can apply a late cancellation, and it's the fee that makes it a late cancellation rather than an ordinary one. The fees themselves are set up once under Settings → Fees.
          The other half — make the cancellation reasons do the counting

          Cancellation reasons are chosen at cancel time and they show up in reports (never in the client's email). If the reason list includes entries like "Client cancellation — 1st free" and "Client cancellation — 2nd free", the count becomes reportable across the whole practice instead of living in one therapist's head.

          Decision for you, Kerry: half two needs the reason list edited once, centrally. Worth doing — it turns a policy nobody can audit into a number on a report.

          Sources: Special Notes · Putting Tags to Work · Cancel or Delete an Appointment

          08Moving one appointment›
          Same day, or between staff — drag it
          1. Click and hold the appointment.
          2. Drag it to the new time, day, or staff column.
          3. Let go. Jane asks you to confirm the move, or to confirm and notify the client.
          A different day — use Move
          1. Click the appointment to open the panel.
          2. Click Move. A bar confirms you're rescheduling.
          3. Navigate with the arrows or Go to Date. Press L to change location.
          4. Click the new time slot on the gridlines.
          Jane never notifies the client on its own. Both routes give you the choice, and it's a real choice — decide, don't click through it.
          Kaiser client? You're only half done. Change it in Lucet too, by hand — nothing syncs. The TPI fires 30 minutes before whatever Lucet says, so until you change it there, the client gets a TPI for the old time and nothing for the new one.

          Source: Jane — Booking, Changing or Moving an Appointment

          09A client moves to a new day or time — changing all the future ones›
          Set expectations here: Jane has no "edit all future occurrences." A standing Tuesday 3pm can't be dragged to Thursday 5pm as a block. You delete the future ones and book a fresh series.
          1. Click any one of the client's appointments to open the panel.
          2. Click the » button next to Move to open Book Recurring Appointments.
          3. The panel lists every date from this appointment forward, each marked Booked, Available or Conflict. Push Repeat Until far enough ahead that the whole existing run appears.
          4. Clear the old run with Delete N Booked Appointment at the bottom left. There is no per-row delete in this panel.
          5. Book a new recurring series on the new day and time.
          6. Kaiser client: open Lucet and edit the recurring appointment to the new day and time, or the TPIs keep firing against the old slot for the rest of the year.
          Deleting is silent. No email goes to the client and no cancellation reason is recorded. Tell the client yourself, and leave a note on the first new appointment saying what moved and when.

          Sources: Cancel or Delete an Appointment · Recurring Appointments

          10A client terminates or stops coming — clearing their future appointments›

          Same panel as 09:

          1. Click one of their appointments → » beside Move.
          2. Set Repeat Until past their last appointment so every booked date shows in the list.
          3. Delete N Booked Appointment at the bottom left clears them in one go.
          Choose deliberately between delete and cancel. Jane's own wording: upcoming appointments "can't be cancelled in bulk; they can only be deleted." Delete sends nothing and records no reason. If you need the client notified, the reason captured for reporting, or a late-cancellation fee charged, cancel them one at a time through Cancel/Delete → Cancel with Notifications.

          Rule of thumb: a planned termination — delete the block, it's cleaner. A client who vanished, or one where fees are in play — cancel individually so the record shows what happened.

          Kaiser client? Cancel the Lucet series too. Use CANCEL APPOINTMENT on the recurring entry. Left alone, Lucet goes on sending that person a TPI half an hour before a session they no longer have — every week, until the series end date.

          Source: Jane — Cancel or Delete an Appointment

          11Keeping the schedule a month ahead — and the reminders that make it stick›
          The therapist's job
          1. Book the next appointment in the room, before the client leaves. Nothing else works as reliably.
          2. For anyone weekly, book a recurring series rather than one at a time.
          3. Check your own forward book — see the keys below.
          Looking four weeks ahead, properly

          Jane has no month view. It has Day View and Week View only, so "a month ahead" means four weeks in Week View:

          1. Click your own name in the left sidebar of the Schedule. It opens in Week View by default, showing seven days side by side.
          2. Press N to jump forward a week. Press it four times and you're looking at a month from now.
          3. Look down your column for empty slots — that's the whole check.
          4. Press T to snap back to today.

          The other keys worth knowing: P goes back a week and 1–7 sets how many days you're viewing at once. To see everyone working today, use the Staff button at the bottom of the schedule — there's a Go To Date button beside it if you'd rather pick a date from a calendar than count weeks.

          Tested 31 August. Clicking your name in the sidebar opens your own Week View, and N, P, T and the number keys all behave as written — one press of N moves exactly one week, so four presses really is a month. A Shift+T shortcut couldn't be confirmed, which is why the Staff button is what's written above.
          Do this on a Thursday, not on the 31st. Four weeks out is far enough that a gap is still fillable by the client you're seeing tomorrow. Found at month end, the same gap is already next month's problem.
          The series runs out before four weeks — extending it

          Jane has no "change the end date." A recurring series is created with an end date and Jane doesn't document a way to edit it afterwards. You don't need to delete anything, though — you extend by booking a fresh run from where the old one stops:

          1. Find the client's last booked appointment. Quickest way: click any of their appointments, open their Appointments tab from the client profile — it lists every appointment with its state and date, and filters by date range.
          2. Click that last appointment to open its panel.
          3. Hit » beside Move to open Book Recurring Appointments.
          4. Set the same day and time pattern, with a new end date further out.
          5. Work through anything marked Conflict or Staff Member Unavailable, then book.
          6. Check the first occurrence isn't a duplicate of the appointment you started from — that's the one thing this method can get wrong.
          Kaiser client? Lucet works the other way, and it's easier. There you can edit the end date: open the recurring appointment, EDIT, and change Ends → On Date to the new date. No rebooking, no duplicates. Do both — extending in Jane without extending in Lucet gives you sessions with no TPI.

          Jane's guides don't document editing an existing series, so the extension method above is the practical route rather than a documented feature. Worth one person confirming it in the account before it goes to everyone. Source: Jane — Recurring Appointments

          Source: Jane — Working With the Schedule

          Jane can nudge, using Tasks
          1. Type into any Note field, then click the speech bubble toggle icon to turn it into a Task.
          2. Set a due date with Due….
          3. Assign it with Assign to Staff Member….
          4. A notification badge appears next to their name when a task is overdue or due within 36 hours.
          5. They see it under their name → My Tasks, and you can see everything under Staff Profile → Tasks.
          Worth testing before you rely on it: Jane's guides don't document Tasks as recurring. If a month-end task doesn't repeat itself, an admin creating twelve dated tasks at the start of the year — or a recurring calendar invite outside Jane — is the more dependable version.
          The admin's job — catching an empty calendar before it costs money
          • Unscheduled Patient Report (Last Visit) — built for exactly this. Filter by staff member and days since last visit to see who isn't booked forward. Run it weekly.
          • Appointments report — set the date range to today through +30 days, filter by practitioner, export to CSV. This is the forecasting number.
          • Hours Scheduled / Booked — gives a % Booked per therapist, the fastest single read on who's thin. Confirm in the account that it accepts future date ranges; the guide isn't explicit.
          One setting to check: under Settings → Online Booking there's an upcoming appointments limit per client. If it's set low, front desk can be quietly blocked from booking a client's fifth session forward — which would look exactly like a therapist not booking ahead.

          Sources: Tasks or To Dos · Unscheduled Patient Report · Appointments Reports · Hours Scheduled / Booked

          12Kaiser's clinical documentation requirements — the deadlines that aren't ours›
          These come from Kaiser, not from Beachside, and they run on their own clocks. They sit alongside everything else on this page — meeting our internal standard does not mean you have met Kaiser's.
          • Initial Evaluation — completed within 72 hours of the first session.
          • Safety Plan Intervention — completed immediately when required: C-SSRS ≥ 3, or when clinically indicated.
          • Discharge Summary — completed at the end of the episode of care.
          • Free-Form Notes — as needed, for clinical updates.
          What that means in practice
          • 72 hours is not a week. A Kaiser client seen on Friday needs their Initial Evaluation by Monday. Our own treatment-plan rule — during the client's first week — is more generous, so for Kaiser clients the 72-hour clock is the one that governs.
          • C-SSRS ≥ 3 triggers a same-day obligation. The score appears on the assessment row in the client's Lucet file, so it is visible before you see them. If you're seeing a Kaiser client and a TPI came back, look at the C-SSRS before the session, not after.
          • Use the Beachside Safety Plan Summary template in Jane for the clinical record, and complete Kaiser's requirement in Lucet. Both, not either.
          • Discharge summaries close the episode. When you clear a client's future appointments (cheat sheet 10), that's the same moment the discharge summary is due — and the same moment to cancel their Lucet series.
          There's also a PAAS obligation sitting in Lucet — the Provider Appointment Availability Survey, an annual California DMHC assessment of timely access. Kaiser, Forvis Mazars or HSAG may contact a provider and ask for their next available appointment; for urgent needs the standard is an available appointment within 48 hours, not business days. If you're contacted about it, tell Kerry rather than answering off the cuff.
          13"Is this actually safe?" — for anyone uneasy about the recording›

          If you're hesitant about recording sessions, that instinct is doing its job. Here is what's true, so you can decide from facts rather than unease.

          Where it happens
          All of this takes place inside HIPAA-compliant software. The recording, the transcription and the finished note stay within Jane. Nothing is pasted into a consumer AI tool, nothing leaves the system you already trust with the whole chart, and Jane states the data is not used to train AI models. It is the same platform holding your clients' records today — this is one more feature inside it, not a new door out.
          What is kept, and for how long
          The transcription is deleted. Automatically, as soon as the note is generated. It is not archived, not retained for review, and not available to anyone later. What survives the session is the note you verified and signed — no audio, no word-for-word record of what was said in the room. If that is the part you were worried about, it is already the answer.
          • The session is transcribed, much as a court reporter would.
          • Jane writes that transcript up in SOAP format.
          • The transcription is deleted.
          • You verify the note, complete the form above it, and sign.
          What stays yours
          • The clinical judgement. The machine reports what was said. What it means is yours, and the form above the SOAP is where that lives.
          • The accuracy. You read it and correct it before signing. It is your record and your signature.
          • The choice. Consent is asked for every time and a client can withdraw it at any point. And you can simply not use it — for a particular client, a particular session, or at all. Nobody has to justify that.
          If a client asks

          Plain and unhurried works better than a policy paragraph: "I can use a tool that listens and drafts my notes, so I'm not writing while we talk. It stays inside our records system, the recording is deleted once the note is written, and I check and correct it myself. I'd like to use it — is that alright with you?" Then let them answer. Most people say yes. Some ask a question or two. A few say no, and that's a complete answer.

          The honest case for using it. It doesn't make you a better clinician. What it does is take the note off the end of your day, which is where burnout tends to accumulate in this work — and it lets you look at the person instead of the keyboard. If that isn't worth it to you, don't use it.
          14Your SOAP note does not live in the same place as the treatment plan›
          House rule, and the simplest way to never have this problem: always open your note from the client's appointment — never from the charting page. Both routes let you write a perfectly good note. Only one of them attaches it to the session. Start from the appointment, every time, and the rest of this item is just background.
          This one has already caught someone out, and it looked like a compliance problem when it wasn't. Notes written every session, within 24 hours, complete — and the schedule showed zero charts, because they were filed in the treatment plan and never attached to the appointments. The work was done. Nobody could see it.
          The difference, in one line each
          • A chart entry is the session note. It belongs to one appointment — that's what makes it show up on the schedule and in every report.
          • A treatment plan is a folder that groups notes together with the diagnosis codes and visit count. It is not where a session note is written.

          A note can be in both. But it only counts as done if it is attached to the appointment — Jane's own rule is that a visit counts toward a plan when it is arrived and linked to a chart entry in that plan.

          The right way — six steps, every session
          1. Open the Schedule (Day or Week view) and find the session you're writing up.
          2. Click the appointment itself. Its panel opens on the right. This single step is what ties the note to the session — everything else follows from it.
          3. Check the appointment is marked Arrived. If it isn't, mark it now.
          4. Start the note from that panel — New Chart Entry — and pick your template: Beachside SOAP Note, or Beachside SOAP Note- for use with AI if you're transcribing.
          5. Fill out the form above the SOAP, write or verify the SOAP, then click Sign and OK.
          6. Glance back at the appointment on the Schedule. It should now carry a padlock — closed means signed and linked. That padlock is your receipt.
          The route to avoid: opening the client's Chart tab and clicking New Chart Entry there, with no appointment open. You will get a complete, dated, signable note that belongs to the client but to no session — which is exactly the invisible-note problem. Same for starting one inside a treatment plan.
          The thirty-second check that catches this

          Open your own week in the Schedule and look along your appointments. Every session you've written up should have a padlock. An appointment with no padlock has no note attached to it — whatever you may have written elsewhere. It's the fastest way to know where you stand, and it takes half a minute.

          Moving a note onto the right appointment — the fix
          Confirmed with Jane, 31 August. This is documented behaviour, not a fault in our account and not a setting anyone forgot to switch on. Jane's own guide says it links a chart entry to an appointment "if the entry had been started from the practitioner's Day Sheet." Start one anywhere else and Jane has no way to know which session you meant, so it stays unattached. The good news is that it can be put right in about thirty seconds, and nothing has to be rewritten.
          Only the person who wrote the note can do this. Jane lets the chart's author change which appointment an entry belongs to — and nobody else. Not an admin, not the office manager, not Kerry. If it's your note, it's your two clicks.
          1. Open the client's chart: Clients → search their name → Chart tab.
          2. Find the entry. It's filed under the date you wrote it, which isn't always the date of the session — so look at when you wrote it, not when you saw them.
          3. Click the arrow at the right-hand end of the entry's grey header bar, beside your name. Its tooltip reads Chart entry options.
          4. A short menu opens: Print, Duplicate, Move to plan, Add Appointment. Choose Add Appointment. (On an entry that is already attached to the wrong session, this reads Change appointment instead.)
          5. Pick the right appointment from the list.
          6. Check it worked. Go to that session's date on the Schedule. The entry should now sit against the appointment, carrying a padlock if it was already signed.
          Tested 31 August on the Ted Test profile. A note started from the Chart tab did exactly what this item describes — it saved with an open padlock and a Draft badge and no session attached. The arrow menu on that entry contained Add Appointment, as written. The same menu also carries Move to plan, which is how a note gets filed into or out of a treatment plan — worth knowing if yours ended up inside one.
          A signed note can still be relinked. Signing doesn't freeze the appointment connection, so you don't need an amendment just to attach it. What signing does lock is the date of service — if that's the thing that's wrong, use the Amendment workflow instead, which keeps the original signed-at timestamp and updates the service date.
          Already have notes sitting in treatment plans, or written from the Chart tab? Don't rewrite them and don't delete anything — the work is good and it is all still there. Work through them with the six steps above, one at a time, oldest first, ticking each off as the padlock appears. If something looks off — an entry you can't find, one that seems to belong to two sessions, or a note that isn't yours — stop there and tell Kerry or Veronica rather than guessing.

          Source: Jane — Treatment Plans · Charting Basics

          The route that works, click by click. Confirmed in our own account on 1 September.
          1. Open the calendar and click the client's appointment. It can be a month ago — that is fine.
          2. The panel opens on the right showing Arrive and No Show. Scroll down to Booking Information.
          3. Click the client's name. A teal panel reading View slides in from the right — it is teal, not green. Click it.
          4. You are now in the client's profile. Click Chart, then New Chart Entry.
          5. Pick the note from the menu. The note opens already matched to the date of service, because you started at the appointment.
          Do not click the first AI option you see. Jane's own Smart SOAP Note and Smart SOAP sit above ours in that menu, both marked with a sparkle. They are not Beachside templates. Choosing one skips the Beachside questions above the note, including the required Client Location field. Scroll down to Beachside SOAP Note - for use with AI.
          15Waiting to hear back about a reschedule — how to keep track of it›
          Jane has no "pending" status. An appointment is Booked, Arrived, Cancelled, No Show, Rescheduled — there is nothing that means "I've asked, they haven't answered." So a reschedule you're waiting on lives in your head until the client replies, and that's where they get lost. Notes are how you get it out of your head and into Jane.
          The note feature itself — how it works

          One tool, two jobs. Learn it once and it covers reschedules, free cancellations, and anything else you'd otherwise try to remember.

          • Adding one: click an appointment → type into Add Note… → click Add.
          • Where it shows: a speech bubble in the top right corner of that appointment on the Schedule, and in full in the appointment panel, the patient profile, and the invoice window. Never on anything the client sees.
          • The star — click it and both star and note turn orange. The note then appears on every future appointment for that client. Use it for anything that stays true.
          • The three dots beside a note offer Delete only. There is no edit — to change a note, add the new one and delete the old.
          • The toggle turns a note into a Task, which is what gives you a due date, an assignee and a notification. Use it for anything you're waiting on.
          The rule of thumb that decides which you use. Star a fact that stays true — "free cancellations: 1 of 2 used". Task a thing that needs doing — "waiting to hear back about Thursday". Star the standing fact, task the errand. Get those two the right way round and notes stop being clutter and start being a system. Free cancellations are worked through step by step in item 07.
          Step one — write the note on the appointment
          1. On the Schedule, click the appointment in question.
          2. Type into Add Note…. Say what you offered and when you asked — "18 Sep: client asked to move. Offered Tue 3pm or Thu 11am. Awaiting reply."
          3. Click Add.
          4. A speech bubble now shows in the top right corner of that appointment on the Schedule, so you can see at a glance which sessions have something attached.

          Notes are internal. They never appear on anything the patient sees. They show in the appointment panel, the patient profile, and the invoice window.

          Step two — turn it into a Task, so it chases you

          This is the part that makes it a real pending item rather than a note you'll never look at again.

          1. In the note, click the speech bubble toggle icon to turn it into a Task.
          2. Click Due… and set the date you'll chase by. Two days is usually right — long enough to be reasonable, short enough that the slot is still fillable.
          3. Click Assign to Staff Member… — yourself, or front desk if they're making the call.
          4. A notification badge appears beside that person's name when the task is overdue or due within 36 hours.
          5. It lives under their name → My Tasks until it's done.
          Step three — star it only if it should follow the client

          Click the star to the right of a note and both the star and the note turn orange. That note then appears on all of that client's future appointments.

          Don't star a "waiting to hear back" note. The star is for standing facts that stay true — "free cancellations used: 1 of 2", a standing arrangement, something the next person to open the chart must know. A one-off reschedule question, starred, follows that client onto every appointment forever and becomes noise. Star the rule, not the errand.
          Seeing everything you're waiting on

          The Notes report lists notes across the practice, filterable by staff member, creation date, status, and starred. That's your outstanding-reschedules list — the closest thing Jane has to a pending queue. Between that and My Tasks, nothing needs to sit in your head.

          When they answer
          • They take a new time: move the appointment (item 08), update the note with what was agreed, and tick the task complete.
          • They don't reply by the due date: chase once. If a second attempt gets nothing, decide — leave it booked, or cancel it under policy. Either way, write the decision in the note.
          • Kaiser client: change it in Lucet too, or the TPI keeps firing against the old time (item 01).
          Write notes as though the client might one day read them. They're internal and never patient-facing — but records do get requested, and a note written plainly and factually reads well in every context. "Offered two alternatives, awaiting reply" ages far better than a shorthand comment about someone being difficult to pin down.

          Sources: Jane — Special Notes · Tasks or To Dos

          16A client moves a first appointment the front desk booked›

          You have never met this person. The front desk matched them to you for a reason, and a message has landed on your phone at the weekend.

          Nothing is on fire. The appointment is days away. Deal with it Monday and nothing breaks — except the client sits worrying all weekend. Send two lines now, do the work later.

          1. Reply, but do not offer a time yet. "Thanks for letting me know — I'm sorry to hear it. I'll move your first appointment and confirm the new time with you."
          2. Move it. Never cancel, never delete. Click the appointment, click Move, navigate to the new date, click the new slot. Cancelling throws away the booking the front desk built. Deleting is silent, records nothing, and is only ever for an appointment made by mistake.
          3. Jane asks whether to notify. Say yes. For someone who has never met you, written confirmation of the new time is worth a great deal.
          4. Tell the front desk. They booked it and hold the intake forms. A note on the appointment does not reach them.
          5. The intake forms look after themselves. The reminders re-point at the new date on their own — verified in History and Status. Our reminders go out 3 days ahead by email and 2 days ahead by text, not 24 hours (Settings › Reminders & Notifications, checked 2 September).
          6. Your treatment plan is now due a week later — it is due the week the client starts.
          7. If they are on Lucet, move it there too. Nothing syncs, and the TPI fires against whatever Lucet says.
          This does not count against them. A first appointment moved before it ever happens does not use a reschedule and is not one of the two free cancellations. Both clocks start at session one. Set 1 September 2026.
          There is an Undo. Straight after a move, a green bar offers to revert it. It disappears when you navigate away — so if you have just moved the wrong appointment, act immediately.
          Do not assume the client got the notification. Checked 2 September: 590 of 730 clients are subscribed to the email reminder and 418 of 730 to the text. For booking, cancellation and change notifications the split is worse — 87 profiles enabled, 638 disabled. Confirm And Notify is still the right click, but for a first appointment, send the client a line yourself as well. For anyone you have never met, assume nothing reached them.
          17You are sick — and one of today's clients has never met you›

          Same clicks as 16. Different decisions.

          1. Block the day and label the block exactly Sick. Do this first. Breaks are a filterable state, so that one word is what stops a sick day counting against you in booked-versus-seen.
          2. Get the list. Reports → Appointments → your name, today's date, state First Visit. That is everyone booked with you today who has never been seen.
          3. Those people get a phone call, not an email. The front desk rings them with a replacement time already in hand. A first session cancelled by the clinic, with only an automated notice, is one of the most reliable ways to lose a new client before they start.
          4. Everyone else — move, or cancel with notify the client ticked.
          5. Nothing gets billed and nothing counts against anyone. This is the clinic cancelling, not the client.
          6. Kaiser clients — change Lucet, or the TPI goes out for a session that is not happening.
          There is no automatic sick-day email, and Jane cannot build one. Reminders fire only relative to an appointment, there is no send-at-a-time, and there is no way to email a group. Four minutes of phone calls is the process.
          18A client asks to reschedule by text›

          Two texts, not one. That is the whole discipline.

          1. Answer straight away, even before you know your availability. "Thanks for letting me know. Yes, we can move it. I'll text you shortly with the times I have available."
          2. Then send the times, with the deadline in the same message. Two or three options, never a blank "what works for you?" — that is how a reschedule turns into eight messages.
          3. Email the same thing. The text gets read; the email is the record.
          4. Extend the deadline when life is genuinely in the way. Someone sitting in an emergency room is not ignoring you. Say so plainly, and write a note saying you extended it and why.
          5. When they answer, move it (16 for a first appointment, 08 for an existing one), update the note, tick the task closed.
          The deadline. Four hours — and if four hours would land after 9pm, the deadline becomes 9am the next morning. Nobody gets a twenty-minute window and nobody gets texted at midnight.
          Never mention the cancellation count in a text. You cannot know at that moment whether the client's two are already used up. Where the count stands is a conversation for the next session. And a client who has not yet had a first appointment cannot be charged for a reschedule at all.
          Not for sending — why the deadline exists. An unanswered reschedule holds a slot nobody is using. That is the reason for the four hours, and the reason to hold the line on it. It is not a thing to say to a client. If you need to give a reason out loud, "so I can hold one for you" is the honest, kind version.
          19Your client's appointments are running out›
          1. Seeing it before it bites. Click any of the client's appointments → the » button next to Move → Book Recurring Appointments . The panel lists dates from this appointment forward and marks the ones already Booked. For the definitive list, open the client's Appointments tab — every appointment, with its state, filterable by date range.
          2. Adding more. Book a fresh recurring series starting the week after the current one ends. Jane will not extend an existing series — you are adding a second run alongside it.
          3. Check the authorisation before you book past it. Booking twenty more in Jane does not mean twenty are covered.
          4. Kaiser clients — extend the Lucet series too. The two have separate end dates and nothing syncs. When the Lucet one runs out the TPIs simply stop, silently.
          5. Treatment plan check. Reports → Treatment Plans shows visits against suggested visits. A client well past their suggested number is a clinical decision before it is a scheduling one.
          If » seems to do nothing, read the red bar at the top. "Please select an appointment booked within a shift to add recurring appointments" means the appointment is sitting outside your published availability, so Jane has no shift to repeat it into. Publish the shift, or move the appointment inside one, and the panel opens normally. Verified in our account on 3 September.
          20A client whose availability keeps moving — shift workers›

          The surgeon on rotating shifts, the nurse, the firefighter, the parent on split childcare. Jane has no concept of "flexible", so this is handled by convention.

          1. Do not book a recurring series. It will be wrong within a fortnight. Book individual appointments.
          2. Star a note on the client so it follows them onto every appointment: "Shift work — books month by month, confirm dates at end of each month."
          3. Spend ten minutes at the start or end of a session reviewing the next few weeks together. Doctors and nurses usually have their rota one to two months ahead — the information exists, it just needs asking for.
          4. Put them in your month-end routine by name. They get a call or a text, not an assumption.
          5. Use the Wait List as a backup for someone who can sometimes take a short-notice slot.
          Why this matters beyond the one client. A shift worker leaves gaps in your column, and those gaps look identical to a therapist who simply is not booking ahead. The starred note is what tells anyone reading the schedule which one they are looking at.
          21A no show, or a late cancellation — which button, and why the amount changes›

          A no show is when they do not come and do not call. If they ring afterwards to explain, it is still a no show for billing. What changes the billing is whether you reschedule it.

          Rescheduled it? Use the zero-dollar option. No Show - with reschedule ($0.00) records the no show without charging. Same on the cancellation side: Cancelation- Rescheduled ($0.00). The event is still on the record — you are choosing not to charge for it, which is not the same as pretending it did not happen.

          Check the insurance before you pick the fee

          House rule. We cannot charge a client more for a no show than the insurer reimburses, including their copay. That is why there is a separate fee for every payer rather than one flat amount — pick the one that matches their plan, not the generic one.

          Verified in Settings › Billing › Fees on 3 September:

          • No Show $125.00 · No Show - Self Pay $110.00 · No-Show First Appointment $110.00
          • Kaiser $110.00 · Beacon/Carelon $131.97 · Aetna $111.23 · Anthem $111.22 · Optum $121.33 · Blue Shield $84.00 · Cigna/Evernorth $111.00 · Other $110.00

          We do not offer cancellation. We offer rescheduling.

          That is the policy, and it changes what you do the moment the message arrives. There is no "cancel" outcome a client is entitled to — there is a reschedule, and a fee only when a reschedule turns out to be impossible.

          The cancel control sits on the appointment screen below Booking Information. Click Cancel/Delete and a dropdown opens — but that is the last step, not the first.

          1. Notice in advance? It is a reschedule. Offer times. Nothing is charged and nothing is cancelled. Item 18 has the two-text discipline for doing this by message.
          2. Last minute — under 24 hours — try to accommodate a reschedule first. This is a real step, not a formality. Look at your week and offer what you actually have.
          3. Only if you genuinely cannot accommodate one does it become a late cancellation, and only then is anything charged. The fee is the fallback when rescheduling fails, not the standard response to short notice.
          4. Rescheduled it after all? Record it with Cancelation- Rescheduled ($0.00). The event stays on the record and the client is not charged. That entry exists precisely because rescheduling is the default.
          5. Charging? Match their payer, same rule as a no show. Late Cancelation $125.00 · Kaiser $110.00 · Anthem $111.22 · Aetna $111.23 · Beacon/Carelon $131.97 · Cigna/Evernorth $111.00 · Optum $121.33 · Blue Shield $84.00.
          6. Any fee button opens a second screen asking for the reason. Choose it there.
          Why the order matters. A therapist who reaches for the fee button on a last-minute message has skipped the part the client is actually owed. Offer the time first. If you have nothing to offer, the fee is fair and the record will show you tried.

          The two freebies

          Every client earns two freebies a year once they have three months of regular attendance behind them. New clients do not have them; the clock starts after that first quarter.

          A freebie is deliberately flexible. It can stand in for a late cancellation fee, for a no show fee, or for a reschedule — whichever the client needs it for. It is not three separate allowances, it is two uses of one allowance.

          1. Open Cancel/Delete and choose Cancel Appointment - No Charge.
          2. On the screen that follows, mark that they are using their first or second freebie of the year.
          Say it out loud to the client. "I'm using one of your two for the year" is worth saying, because the second one lands very differently if they did not know the first was spent. Item 18 still applies — never raise the count in a text, where you cannot see their face and may not have checked.
          Check the count before you spend one. Jane has no per-client freebie counter. Keep it on a starred note on the client — see item 07 — and read it before you tell anyone what they have left.
          Jane's window is set to 48 hours. Our policy is 24. Settings › Billing › Fees says in as many words: "Your time period for the cancellation policy is set up for 48 hours." So for a cancellation somewhere between 24 and 48 hours out, Jane will offer you the late-cancellation fee buttons for something we do not charge for. The buttons appearing is not permission to use them. Under 24 hours, no reschedule — that is the test, not what Jane shows you.
          Two buttons you may go looking for and not find. There is a No Show Other for a reason that is not listed, but there is no equivalent on the cancellation side — no "Late Cancelation Other". There is also no self-pay late-cancellation fee, though No Show - Self Pay exists. If you need either, use the closest match and write the reason in a note, and tell Kerry so the fee can be added.
          Blue Shield is filed under the wrong word. The entry reads Last Cancelation- Blue Shield, not "Late". If you are scanning the list alphabetically for a Blue Shield client, that is why you cannot see it.
          Never delete instead of cancelling. Deleting records nothing and sends nothing. A no show or a late cancellation is exactly the event you want on the record.

          Cheat sheet visual

          The same steps, in pictures, for anyone who would rather see it than read it. The numbers match the written cheat sheet exactly — item 14 here is item 14 there. The green ring marks the thing to click.

          About these screenshots. Every screen is real, from our own Jane account. The client shown is a test record made for this walkthrough — he is not a person. Where another therapist's column appears, those clients are blurred. Jane does not do that for you: do it yourself before you ever screenshot a schedule.
          14Starting a note so Jane links it to the session›

          A note started in the wrong place is complete, signed, and invisible to the schedule and to every report. It looks to everyone else like you never wrote it.

          14.01   Always start at the appointment

          Open the calendar and click the client's appointment. It can be a month ago — that is fine. Starting here is what tells Jane which session the note belongs to.

          14.02   The panel opens on the right

          You will see Arrive and No Show at the top. Scroll down to Booking Information.

          14.03   Click the client's name

          A teal panel reading View slides in from the right. Click it. (It is teal, not green — do not go hunting for a green square.)

          14.04   You are now in the client's profile

          The tab row appears: Profile, Edit / Settings, Chart, Medications, Appointments, Billing and the rest.

          14.05   Click Chart, then New Chart Entry

          New Treatment Plan sits beside it. They are not the same thing — a SOAP note filed inside a treatment plan will not link to the session.

          14.06   Do not stop at the first AI option

          Jane's own Smart SOAP Note and Smart SOAP appear first, with sparkle icons. They are not ours. Picking one skips the Beachside questions above the note, including the required Client Location field.

          14.07   Scroll to the Beachside templates

          Transcribing? Beachside SOAP Note - for use with AI. In person? Beachside SOAP Note. Every note type is in this menu. The note opens already matched to the date of service, because you started from the appointment.

          16A client moves a first appointment›

          You have never met this person. The front office matched them to you for a reason, and a message has landed on your phone at the weekend.

          16.01   Find the appointment

          The First Visit badge marks a client who has never been seen. It matters — nothing counts against a client whose care has not started.

          16.02   This is the board you will actually see

          Every therapist's column, side by side. Other clients are blurred here for privacy — Jane does not do that for you.

          16.03   Move it. Never delete it.

          Copy, Move, » and Cancel/Delete sit under the booking details. Move keeps the booking the front office built. Delete is silent, records nothing, and is only ever for an appointment booked by mistake.

          16.04   Jane tells you what it is waiting for

          An orange bar names the client, the therapist and the original time, and waits for you to click an open slot. Cancel Move backs out safely. You can navigate to another week and the move stays live.

          16.05   Notifying is a real choice

          Confirm, or Confirm And Notify. For someone who has never met you, a written confirmation of the new time is worth a great deal. Choose deliberately — do not click through it.

          16.06   There is an Undo

          The green bar offers to revert the change. It disappears when you navigate away, so if you have just moved the wrong appointment, act now.

          16.07   The reminder follows the new date by itself

          History and Status records who moved what and when, and shows the email reminder re-pointed at the new date. You do not need to touch the intake forms.

          16.08   But do not assume it reached them

          Our reminders go 3 days ahead by email and 2 days by text — not 24 hours. And the subscription numbers matter: 590 of 730 clients get the email, 418 of 730 get the text, and for booking or change notifications only 87 profiles are enabled against 638 disabled. Confirm And Notify is still right. For someone you have never met, send them a line yourself as well.

          08What Jane will and will not let you do›

          Two things worth seeing with your own eyes, because they change what you can promise a client.

          08.01   The Cancel menu offers no fee

          Cancel with Notifications gives one option — Cancel Appointment - No Charge. Without notifications, Delete Appointment. There is no fee choice on an appointment booked well ahead.

          08.02   But the fees do exist

          Settings › Billing › Fees already holds four named scenarios, including Late Cancellation and Cancel without Reschedule. They surface only when a cancellation falls inside the window set in Jane.

          15Waiting to hear back about a reschedule›

          Jane has no “pending” status. An appointment is Booked, Arrived, Cancelled, No Show or Rescheduled — there is nothing that means “I have asked, they have not answered.” Notes are how you get it out of your head and into Jane.

          15.01   Decide star or task BEFORE you click Add

          The star and the task toggle sit above the box while you are typing. Star a fact that stays true. Toggle to a task for something you are waiting on. Get this right first time — the choice is easiest here.

          15.02   The saved note stamps itself

          It records who wrote it, when, and which appointment it belongs to. Notes never appear on anything the client sees. Write them as though the client might one day read them anyway — records do get requested.

          17You are sick — finding today's new patients›

          When you cannot work, the people who have never met you are the ones at risk of disappearing. This is how you find them in under a minute.

          17.01   Reports → Appointments

          The whole day, every therapist, every state. Filter it down rather than scrolling.

          17.02   Filter the state to First Visit

          Unarrived, Booked Online, Checked In, Arrived, No Show, Rescheduled — and further down, First Visit. Add your own name and today's date and what is left is exactly the people who have never been seen. Those get a phone call, not an email.

          19Your client's appointments are running out›

          A run of appointments ends quietly. Nobody is told. The first sign is usually a client saying "I don't think I have anything booked" — by which point you have lost a week.

          19.01   The » button is Book Recurring Appointments

          It sits between Move and Cancel/Delete and has no label — hover and Jane names it. If it refuses, read the red bar: "Please select an appointment booked within a shift." That is the answer, not a fault. The appointment is sitting outside your published availability, so Jane has nothing to repeat it into.

          19.02   Pick the days, then how far ahead

          Recur On ticks the weekday. Repeat Until sets the end date — Jane defaults to about a month. Frequency handles fortnightly. Change Repeat Until before you look at anything else; everything below it recalculates.

          19.03   Jane checks every week for you

          Each date comes back Available or Conflict, and a Conflict is not a dead end — the dropdown offers the other open times that day. Fix it here rather than booking and cleaning up afterwards.

          19.04   Book them all at once — and this is also how you clear them

          The green button books every date you approved. Beside it, Delete Booked Appointment removes the ones already made. That button is the answer when a client terminates and you need their future slots back.

          11Who has quietly stopped booking›

          Every therapist believes they know who has drifted. Two reports tell you in fifteen seconds, and they are almost never who you expected.

          11.01   Reports → Unscheduled Clients (Last Visit)

          Everyone with no next appointment booked, grouped by therapist, newest gap first. Client names are blurred here. Run it every Monday: a client three weeks past their last session, with nothing booked, has usually not decided to stop — they have just not been asked.

          11.02   And the Wait List is nearly empty

          One person, across the whole practice. The Wait List is where someone who could take a short-notice slot should sit — it is what turns a late cancellation back into a session instead of a gap. Worth raising at the meeting.

          07Counting the two free cancellations›

          Jane will not do this for you. There is no cancellation counter anywhere in the product — which is why the count has to live somewhere you will actually see it.

          07.01   The profile counts bookings and no-shows. Not cancellations.

          Total Bookings, Upcoming Appointments, No Shows — and nothing for cancellations. That gap is the whole reason for the workaround: keep a starred note on the client reading "Cancellations used: 1 of 2 (14 Aug)" and update it the day it happens. A starred note follows the client onto every appointment, so you see it before you reply to a text.

          07.02   The scale of it, practice-wide

          Settings › Dashboard. August: 658 arrived, 119 cancelled, 29 no-shows. Roughly one cancellation for every five sessions kept. Nobody is currently counting these per client, which is what the two-free rule needs in order to mean anything.

          Everything you tick or type saves in this browser only.
